\chapter{Synthesis --- The Decoder}
\label{ch:synthesis-sound-laws}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decode unfamiliar Spanish with three sound laws and three endings.}

Complete ES-C57-sintesis-descifrar: decode hoja and lleno, read a two-ending phrase, and say what a word that resists every rule suggests.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the decoder}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-sintesis-descifrar}



\begin{quote}
Three sound laws and three endings. Before the practice: what do you do with an unfamiliar word starting \emph{h-}? And one starting \emph{ll-}?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you see} & \textbf{what to try} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\emph{-ch-} & Latin \emph{-ct-} & \emph{noche} $\to$ \textbf{nocturnal} \\
\emph{h-} & put an \emph{f} back & \emph{hijo} $\to$ \textbf{filial} \\
\emph{ll-} & try \emph{cl-}, \emph{pl-}, \emph{fl-} & \emph{llave} $\to$ \textbf{clavicle} \\
\emph{-ción} & \emph{-tion} & \emph{nación} $\to$ \textbf{nation} \\
\emph{-dad} & \emph{-ty} & \emph{ciudad} $\to$ \textbf{city} \\
\emph{-mente} & \emph{-ly} & \emph{claramente} $\to$ \textbf{clearly} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six rules, and between them they will get you through a great deal of written Spanish this book has no room to teach.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a decoder is not}]
It is worth being exact about what you have, because overclaiming it will disappoint you at the worst moment.

This is a \textbf{reading} tool, and mostly a first-guess one. It will not tell you how to say something you want to say, it will not give you gender or conjugation, and it will occasionally point at the wrong English word.

What it does is remove the feeling that an unfamiliar Spanish word is a wall. Most of the time it is not a wall — it is a word you already know, wearing clothes you have now learned to recognise. That change of expectation is worth more than any individual word in this chapter, because it is what lets you read something above your level and get most of it.

\textbf{And when the decoder fails, that is information too.} A word that resists every rule is usually from one of Spanish's non-Latin layers — Arabic, Basque, or the Americas — worth noticing precisely because it breaks a rule you hold.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the six rules, in order
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hoja, lleno, noche\textquotedblright{} and name the law behind each
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many rules do you now hold? (\textbf{Six} — three laws and three endings.) What are they for? (\textbf{Reading}, mostly first guesses.) And what has really changed? (An unfamiliar word is \textbf{no longer a wall}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
